name: Neil Kinnock
role: Leader of the British Labour Party and Leader of the Opposition (1983-1992); MP for Bedwellty and Islwyn (1970-1995); European Commissioner (1995-2004)
summary: Kinnock led the Labour Party from 1983 to 1992, moving it from the left toward the centre-left after the 1983 defeat. In the local Commons record he defends the NHS, opposes market tests in schooling and the sell-off of public industries, backs UN authority for force and pooled sovereignty in the European Community, and rejects political violence in Northern Ireland while seeking Irish unity only by consent. Most of his Commons speeches are opposition questions and attacks on the government, so many of the statements find no stated position in the texts checked.

abortion-legal.rationale: In the 1990 Commons abortion votes he opposed the clause cutting the time limit and the 18-, 20- and 22-week amendments, and backed the 26- and 28-week alternatives.

assisted-dying.rationale: As a peer he voted against postponing Lord Joffe's assisted dying bill for six months, letting it go to second reading.

common-currency.rationale: In 2000 he expected Britain to be inside the single currency within five years and said the pound and euro were heading to the outer edge of their practicality.

death-penalty.rationale: Voted against restoring the death penalty in 1983, including for terrorist murders, and again against new clauses to restore it in 1990 and 1994.

decide-locally.rationale: Said he has always been in favour of devolution and decentralisation of power.

direct-action.rationale: Said that politicians who do not do what they can to convince the electorate and win are treating politics as a hobby.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Backed the Anglo-Irish Agreement's principle that Northern Ireland's status changes only with the consent of its majority, which he said alone can decide on unity.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Said the will of the United Nations must prevail over Iraq, and pointed to enforcement under the UN Charter (art. 42) through the Security Council.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Said the obligation to extend rights applies to all individuals without prejudice or preference regardless of race, colour and creed.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Called the EC's 3% deficit limit much too rigid and impractical to be accepted.

force-without-un.rationale: Argued that further military action over Kuwait without further UN authority would cost legitimacy and international-law standing.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: His 1987 manifesto pledged to decommission Polaris and cancel Trident, ending the nuclear pretence.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: As a peer he voted to annul the 2013 regulations opening NHS commissioning to competitive tendering.

national-law-over-international.rationale: As a peer he voted to require that the Rwanda scheme keep full compliance with domestic and international law.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Condemned the IRA and INLA "gunmen" and "men of violence", whose terrorism he said the Anglo-Irish Agreement must defeat.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Told the Commons sovereignty is influence multiplied by active engagement with others, and that sharing power in the European Community makes Britain count for more.

positive-liberty.rationale: Said freedom must be real and usable, not merely formal, because people have the political rights, economic power and security to be truly emancipated.

priority-to-poor.rationale: As a peer he voted to remove the 1% cap on benefit up-rating.

proportional-representation.rationale: Said he considers a more proportionate system more democratic and regretted the delay to electoral reform.

public-access-to-information.rationale: His 1987 manifesto promised a Freedom of Information Act and repeal of Section Two of the Official Secrets Act.

public-ownership.rationale: Defended the earlier taking of essential industries into public ownership as a practical response to private under-investment and opposed selling off water.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: His 1987 and 1992 manifestos pledged a statutory national minimum wage, set at 3.40 pounds an hour in 1992, to end poverty pay.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Told the Commons that all in Parliament agree the crimes of desecration and race hatred deserve strong condemnation and severe punishment.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: His 1992 manifesto kept ballots before strikes and promised no mass or flying pickets.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Said the Labour party wants Ireland united by consent and is committed to working to secure that consent.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: His 1987 manifesto said Labour would maintain the right to buy for council tenants.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: As a peer he voted against the amendment that would have denied the Same Sex Couples Bill a second reading.

school-vouchers.rationale: Dismissed the open-enrolment "son of vouchers" scheme as the application of market forces to school places, a supermarket system with a corner-shop budget.

second-chamber.rationale: In the 2007 Lords reform votes he backed a reformed House with 50%, 60% and 80% elected members.

separated-powers.rationale: Praised 1688 for establishing parliamentary control over the executive, the rule of law and an independent judiciary as the foundations of liberty.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In the 1989 Budget reply he called a Budget that gave the top 1% £16bn of tax cuts against £10bn for the bottom half neither just, efficient nor right.

turn-back-illegal-migrants.rationale: As a peer he voted against an amendment requiring refusal of asylum claims from illegal entrants.

unions-good.rationale: As a peer he voted for amendments to soften the political-fund opt-in and to remove clause 13 in the 2016 Trade Union Bill.

vote-at-sixteen.rationale: As a peer he voted to give 16- and 17-year-olds a vote in the EU referendum.

women-suffrage.rationale: Said the democratic obligation to extend rights applies to women as well as men.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Opposed withdrawing benefit from young unemployed people who refuse training schemes, calling it conscription and coercion, and in 1987 called conscripting the young unemployed part of a brutal system long abandoned.

notes: Local-texts pass. The main source is the UK Commons Hansard corpus (1970-1994, 3,790 speeches by Kinnock), searched by topic. It holds speeches, not votes, so every answer rests on words. Most speeches are oppositional questions or attacks on the Thatcher and Major governments, and where they state no position of his own on a statement the answer is null. The 1983-87 unilateral nuclear policy and the 1989 policy review are not settled by any speech found, so the nuclear-weapons statements are null.
